where: section 3, sentence 'AccessController tests the current domain.'
problem: This contradicts the sentence two lines earlier and the standard behaviour. AccessController.checkPermission does not test only the current (caller's) domain; it walks the whole call stack and checks every ProtectionDomain on it, failing if any one lacks the permission. A student reading 'tests the current domain' will think only the immediate caller is checked, which is wrong and would also make the earlier stack-inspection sentence meaningless.
fix: AccessController walks the call stack and tests every ProtectionDomain on it; if any domain on the stack lacks the permission, the check fails. A doPrivileged block cuts the walk short at that frame.

where: section 1, sentence 'The rights are read, write, execute, or copy.' followed by 'The amplify right lets the holder add rights.'
problem: The list of rights is presented as complete, then a fifth right (amplify) appears without warning. A student may think amplify is one of the four, or may not see how it differs from copy.
fix: The rights are a bit vector, for example read, write, execute and copy. Some systems add an amplify right: the holder may increase the rights when passing on a copy, which plain copy does not allow.

where: section 2, sentence 'the kernel cannot find the child's copy by scanning P's list'
problem: This reads as if scanning P's list might have found the child's copy under other circumstances. Scanning P's list only ever returns P's own entries; that is exactly why copies are untraceable.
fix: the kernel has no record of the child's copy anywhere, so searching P's own list finds nothing.
